\begin{theorem}[Mutation formulae (complete)]
\label{thm:A168-mut}
For skew-symmetric $B$ and index $k$:
\begin{equation}
B'_{ij}
=
\begin{cases}
-B_{ij} & i=k\ \mathrm{or}\ j=k,\\
B_{ij}+\mathrm{sgn}(B_{ik}B_{kj})\cdot|B_{ik}B_{kj}|
& i,j\neq k,\ B_{ik}B_{kj}>0,\\
B_{ij} & i,j\neq k,\ B_{ik}B_{kj}\le 0,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
equivalently A158 formula with the average of absolute products. Cluster variables:
\begin{equation}
x_k x_k'
=
\prod_{B_{ik}>0}x_i^{B_{ik}}
+
\prod_{B_{ik}<0}x_i^{-B_{ik}}.
\end{equation}
Both are involutions: $\mu_k\circ\mu_k=\mathrm{id}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Standard Fomin--Zelevinsky; direct expansion for involution on matrices; exchange relation symmetry for variables.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Soft-mode invariance under every mutation]
\label{thm:A168-soft}
For every $B\in\mathcal{M}(B_{\rm eq})$, the underlying AF dimer count remains $n/2=3$ on $6$ mutable vertices, and soft$(6)=0$ is constant on the class. No mutation creates a soft mode.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Mutation preserves the number of mutable vertices. The AF perfect matching type is a property of the bipartite $C_6$ combinatorial type preserved by the finite mutation class of the alternating exchange matrix (A158). Soft$(n)=|n/2-3|$ depends only on $n=6$. Explicit class: all matrices $6\times 6$ skew with bounded entries, no vertex deletion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Laurent phenomenon + positivity on the full class]
\label{thm:A168-Laurent}
Every cluster variable obtained along any mutation path in $\mathcal{M}(B_{\rm eq})$ is a Laurent polynomial in the initial dual-route seed $x_i^{(0)}=\sqrt{\chi}$ with integer coefficients, positive on the dual-route positive cone.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fomin--Zelevinsky Laurent phenomenon for any seed; positivity by subtraction-free exchange and positive initial data (A158); class finite so every variable appears after finitely many mutations.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tropical mutation dynamics on the class]
\label{thm:A168-trop}
Along any edge $B\xrightarrow{\mu_k}B'$, dual-route valuations $p_i=v_\chi(x_i)$ mutate by
\begin{equation}
p_k'
=
\min\Bigl(\sum_{B_{ik}>0}B_{ik}p_i,\;\sum_{B_{ik}<0}(-B_{ik})p_i\Bigr)-p_k,
\end{equation}
and $p_i'=p_i$ ($i\neq k$). This is compatible with $A$/$X$ tropical dual exchange (A161) on the ensemble locus.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply $v_\chi$ to the exchange relation under dual-route positivity (leading terms do not cancel).
\end{proof}

soft$(n)=0\Leftrightarrow n=6$ for even $n$. Statement of $X_1$ quantifies over the same soft function as Maxwell. O2: $m$ free under $X_1$ only.

The exchange quiver of the continuum packing is of finite mutation type, and the mutable rank equals the number of AF dimers.

\section{SN-A171 --- Quiver Representation Theory of the Packing Seed}
\label{sec:SN-A171}
%==============================================================================

\begin{definition}[Path algebra and representations]
\label{def:A171-rep}
Let $Q$ be the quiver of $B_{\rm eq}$ (vertices $\{0,\dots,5\}$, arrow $i\to j$ with multiplicity $B_{ij}$ when $B_{ij}>0$). A representation $V$ assigns a finite-dimensional $\mathbb{R}$-vector space $V_i$ to each vertex and a linear map $V_a:V_i\to V_j$ to each arrow $a:i\to j$. Dimension vector $\mathbf{d}=(\dim V_i)_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{6}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Euler / Tits form of $B_{\rm eq}$]
\label{def:A171-Tits}
\begin{equation}
q_Q(\mathbf{d})
=
\sum_{i=0}^{5}d_i^2
-
\sum_{B_{ij}>0}B_{ij}\,d_i d_j.
\end{equation}
The Euler form is $\langle\mathbf{d},\mathbf{e}\rangle=\sum d_ie_i-\sum_{B_{ij}>0}B_{ij}d_ie_j$, with $q_Q(\mathbf{d})=\langle\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}\rangle$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Tits form on simple and isotropic roots]
\label{thm:A171-roots}
\begin{enumerate}
\item For each simple root $\mathbf{e}_i$ (standard basis), $q_Q(\mathbf{e}_i)=1$ (real simple roots).
\item For the isotropic vector $\delta=(1,1,1,1,1,1)$, $q_Q(\delta)=0$.
\item Hence the quadratic form is positive semi-definite of corank $1$ on the AF $C_6$ quiver --- affine type signature compatible with finite mutation class of $B_{\rm eq}$ (A168).
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(1) $q(\mathbf{e}_i)=1$ with no arrows contributing inside a single vertex. (2) $\sum d_i^2=6$; arrows of $B_{\rm eq}$: six unit arrows around $C_6$ (each undirected edge contributes one directed term of weight $1$ in the AF orientation pattern with total $\sum_{B_{ij}>0}B_{ij}d_id_j=6$ when $d_i=1$ all $i$). Direct certificate: $q(\delta)=0$. (3) Affine ADE quivers have PSD Tits form with radical spanned by $\delta$; finite mutation type of the exchange matrix is consistent with this affine combinatorial type (A158/A168).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Reflection functors and soft-mode dictionary]
\label{thm:A171-reflect}
Simple reflection $s_i$ at a sink/source acts on dimension vectors by
\begin{equation}
s_i(\mathbf{d})
=
\mathbf{d}-2\frac{\langle\mathbf{e}_i,\mathbf{d}\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{e}_i,\mathbf{e}_i\rangle}\mathbf{e}_i
=
\mathbf{d}-\langle\mathbf{e}_i,\mathbf{d}\rangle\mathbf{e}_i
\quad(q(\mathbf{e}_i)=1).
\end{equation}
Cluster mutation at vertex $i$ on the exchange matrix is compatible with BGP reflection functors at sinks/sources on the quiver of $B_{\rm eq}$. Soft-mode vanishing soft$(6)=0$ corresponds to the absence of negative Tits values on dimension vectors supported on proper AF dimer subconfigurations: every nonzero $\mathbf{d}$ with support size compatible with a single soft mode would force $q_Q(\mathbf{d})<0$ in indefinite type, which does not occur for this PSD form on the Maxwell-selected $n=6$ quiver.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
BGP reflection functors realise mutations at sinks/sources (Brenner--Butler; cluster-tilting literature). PSD of $q_Q$ precludes imaginary roots except multiples of $\delta$; physical soft modes of continuum AF coverings with soft$>0$ correspond to indefinite or defective counts outside this quiver type (A141). Under $H_{\rm cont}$, the packing quiver is fixed as $B_{\rm eq}$, so representation-theoretic root system matches soft$(6)=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Indecomposables and cluster variables]
\label{thm:A171-indec}
For the AF $C_6$ quiver of affine type, indecomposable representations are organised by the root system of $q_Q$: real root dimension vectors give rigid indecomposables; multiples of $\delta$ give regular (tubular) families. Cluster variables of the seed $(\mathbf{x},B_{\rm eq})$ are in bijection with reachable almost-positive roots / cluster-tilting denominators along the mutation class $\mathcal{M}(B_{\rm eq})$ of size $12\,000$ (A168), evaluated at dual-route initial $x_i=\sqrt{\chi}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Affine quiver representation theory (Dlab--Ringel; Kac) + Fomin--Zelevinsky denominator theorem linking cluster variables to roots. Finite labelled mutation class (A168) $\Rightarrow$ finite set of reachable cluster seeds; Laurent census (A172) counts distinct dual-route scalar values.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Quiver rep does not unlock unrestricted closure]
\label{thm:A171-no-unlock}
Representation theory of $B_{\rm eq}$ presupposes the AF $C_6$ quiver selected by $H_{\rm cont}$. It does not derive that quiver from free $\mathcal{A}_0$. O1--O6 stand. \texttt{unrestricted\_open\_system\_closed} remains false.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A169 meta-theorem; quiver input is $\mathcal{A}_2$ structure.
\end{proof}

\section{SN-A174 --- Residual Gross--Pitaevskii + Madelung under Dual-Route $F$}
\label{sec:SN-A174}
%==============================================================================

\begin{definition}[Dual-route residual free-energy (locked)]
\label{def:A174-F}
Under dual-route + $H_{\rm cont}$ + $D_{6h}$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:A174-F}
F[\rho]
=
\int_\Omega
\Biggl(
\rho\log\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}
+
\frac{\kappa_R}{2}(\rho-\rho_\star)^2
+
\xi\,\eta_{\rm leak}\bigl(L[\rho]\bigr)
+
\lambda_{\rm sec}\,\rho_{\rm sec}
\Biggr)\,dV,
\end{equation}
with $\kappa_R=I_W+\chi$, $\xi=\varphi^{-1}$, $\eta_{\rm leak}=\eta_0 e^{-\gamma L}(1+K_{\rm mem}L)$, $\eta_0=\chi$, $K_{\rm mem}=I_W$, $\gamma=\gamma^\star_{C_6}$, and sector indicator dual-route locked (A148/A162).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Residual order parameter and Madelung map]
\label{def:A174-Madelung}
Complex residual order parameter $\psi:\Omega\to\mathbb{C}$ with
\begin{equation}
\rho=|\psi|^2,
\qquad
\psi=\sqrt{\rho}\,e^{iS},
\qquad
v=\nabla S
\end{equation}
(dual-route units with $m=1$, $\hbar=1$). The Madelung map is a diffeomorphism from $\{\psi\neq 0\}$ onto $\{\rho>0\}\times \mathbb{R}/(2\pi\mathbb{Z})$ phase classes.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Residual Gross--Pitaevskii equation]
\label{def:A174-GP}
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:A174-GP}
i\,\partial_t\psi
=
-\frac12\Delta\psi
+
\Bigl(
\kappa_R\bigl(|\psi|^2-\rho_\star\bigr)
+
\log\frac{|\psi|^2}{\rho_0}
+
1
+
\mu_{\rm leak}[L]
+
\mu_{\rm sec}
\Bigr)\psi,
\end{equation}
where chemical potentials are the dual-route functional derivatives
\begin{equation}
\mu_{\rm leak}
=
\xi\,\frac{\delta}{\delta\rho}\int\eta_{\rm leak}(L[\rho])\,dV,
\qquad
\mu_{\rm sec}
=
\lambda_{\rm sec}\frac{\delta\rho_{\rm sec}}{\delta\rho},
\end{equation}
evaluated on $\rho=|\psi|^2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Madelung equivalence to residual hydrodynamics]
\label{thm:A174-equiv}
On $\{\psi\neq 0\}$, equation~\eqref{eq:A174-GP} is equivalent to the residual continuity and Euler system
\begin{align}
\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)
&=
0,
\label{eq:A174-cont}
\\
\partial_t v+(v\cdot\nabla)v
&=
-\nabla\mu
-
\nabla Q,
\label{eq:A174-euler}
\\
\mu
&=
\frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho}
=
\log\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}+1+\kappa_R(\rho-\rho_\star)+\mu_{\rm leak}+\mu_{\rm sec},
\label{eq:A174-mu}
\\
Q
&=
-\frac12\frac{\Delta\sqrt{\rho}}{\sqrt{\rho}}
\quad\text{(dual-route quantum pressure)}.
\label{eq:A174-Q}
\end{align}
In particular, the free-energy open-system flow of A147--A148 is the Madelung hydrodynamics of~\eqref{eq:A174-GP} in the pressure-dominated regime $Q\to 0$ (or after absorbing $Q$ into an extended free-energy $\tilde F=F+\int\frac12|\nabla\sqrt{\rho}|^2$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $\psi=\sqrt{\rho}\,e^{iS}$, $v=\nabla S$. Separate~\eqref{eq:A174-GP} into real and imaginary parts. Imaginary part: continuity~\eqref{eq:A174-cont}. Real part: Hamilton--Jacobi equation for $S$, take gradient: Euler~\eqref{eq:A174-euler} with $\mu=\delta F/\delta\rho$ from~\eqref{eq:A174-F} and quantum pressure~\eqref{eq:A174-Q}. Extended free-energy identity: $\int\frac12|\nabla\sqrt{\rho}|^2$ generates $Q$ as its first variation. $Q\to 0$ recovers pure Wasserstein / residual free-energy gradient flow of A148.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$D_{6h}$ equivariance of residual GP]
\label{thm:A174-D6h}
If $F$ is $D_{6h}$-equivariant (A147) and the Laplacian is the Euclidean Laplacian on a $D_{6h}$-invariant domain (or hexagonal torus), then~\eqref{eq:A174-GP} is $D_{6h}$-equivariant: for $g\in D_{6h}$,
\begin{equation}
\psi(t,x)\ \text{solution}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\psi^g(t,x):=\psi(t,g^{-1}x)\ \text{solution}.
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Delta$ commutes with orthogonal actions; $\rho\mapsto\rho\circ g^{-1}$ preserves $F$ by A147; chemical potentials are natural; hence the GP vector field is equivariant.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sound speed and healing length --- dual-route]
\label{thm:A174-scales}
Linearising~\eqref{eq:A174-GP} about $\psi=\sqrt{\rho_\star}$ yields residual sound speed and healing length
\begin{equation}
c_s=\sqrt{\kappa_R}=\sqrt{I_W+\chi},
\qquad
\xi_{\rm heal}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\kappa_R\rho_\star}}
\quad(\rho_\star=1:\ \xi_{\rm heal}=1/\sqrt{2\kappa_R}).
\end{equation}
Certificate: $c_s\approx 0.9105929973100293$, $\xi_{\rm heal}\approx 0.7764$ (dual-route units).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Standard Bogoliubov expansion of GP with interaction $\kappa_R$ and background $\rho_\star$; dual-route $\kappa_R=I_W+\chi$ locked.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Kinetic + rotational energy identities]
\label{thm:A174-KR}
Along Madelung solutions,
\begin{equation}
E_{\rm kin}
=
\int\frac12\rho|v|^2,
\qquad
\mathbf{L}
=
\int\rho\,x\times v\,dV,
\end{equation}
with $\frac{d}{dt}E_{\rm kin}=-\int\rho v\cdot\nabla(\mu+Q)$ and $D_{6h}$-torque balance for $\mathbf{L}$ when $F$ is equivariant. These realise the kinetic/rotational linkages of the exploration note under dual-route $F$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Multiply Euler by $\rho v$ and integrate (kinetic); cross $x$ into Euler and integrate (angular momentum); equivariance kills external torque from $F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Investigation strengthening]
\label{cor:A174-strengthen}
Madelung/GP is the \textbf{dynamical realisation layer} of residual open-system theory under $H_{\rm cont}$ (exploration v0.1, \S5--6). It does not select soft$(n)=0$ from free $\mathcal{A}_0$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection*{A. Irrep-blocked spectral mesh}

\begin{definition}[$D_{6h}$ residual Hessian operator]
\label{def:A175-H}
On mass-zero residual density perturbations $u$ (real),
\begin{equation}
H_{\rm res}u
=
\frac{\delta^2 F}{\delta\rho^2}\Big|_{\rho_\star}[u]
=
\Bigl(\rho_\star^{-1}+\kappa_R\Bigr)u
+
K_{\rm leak}[u]
+
K_{\rm sec}[u]
-\tfrac12\Delta u,
\end{equation}
with $K_{\rm leak}$ the second variation of leak (A151) and $K_{\rm sec}$ sector Hessian. Quantum-pressure contribution from extended $\tilde F$ is $-\frac12\Delta$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Hexagonal Fourier / irrep mesh]
\label{def:A175-mesh}
On the hexagonal torus $T_\hex=\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda_{\rm hex}$ with dual lattice $\Lambda_{\rm hex}^*$, modes $e^{ik\cdot x}$, $k\in\Lambda_{\rm hex}^*$, are organised by little groups into $D_{6h}$ irreps $\{A_{1g},A_{2g},B_{1g},B_{2g},E_{1g},E_{2g},A_{1u},\ldots\}$ (standard character table). The spectral mesh is
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{spec}(H_{\rm res})
=
\bigsqcup_{\Gamma\in\widehat{D_{6h}}}
\bigsqcup_{k\in\mathcal{O}_\Gamma}
\lambda_\Gamma(k),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{O}_\Gamma$ runs over wavevector orbits transforming as $\Gamma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Irrep block diagonalisation]
\label{thm:A175-block}
$H_{\rm res}$ commutes with the unitary $D_{6h}$ action on $L^2(T_\hex)$, hence is block diagonal in the isotypic decomposition. Equatorial AF doublets sit in $E_{1g}/E_{2g}$ blocks with dual-route floor controlled by $\gamma^\star_{C_6}$ and soft$(6)=0$ (A143/A166). Bulk $A_{1g}$ mass-zero modes have gap $\ge \kappa_R+H_{\rm leak}+R_{\rm nat}$ in the radial Fourier model refined by mesh radius $|k|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Equivariance of $F$ (A147) $\Rightarrow$ equivariance of Hessian. Schur: operators on irreps are scalar on isotypics for 1D irreps and $2\times 2$ blocks for $E$-type. Soft-mode theorem kills zero eigenvalues in $E$-blocks at Maxwell. Bulk lower bound: symbol of $\rho_\star^{-1}+\kappa_R-\frac12\Delta+H_{\rm leak}$ is $\ge \kappa_R+H_{\rm leak}+|k|^2/2$ for $|k|\ge 0$ mass-zero projected modes with dual-route $R_{\rm nat}$ shift from packing sector (A172).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral mesh certificate (hexagonal shell numerics)]
\label{thm:A175-mesh-num}
For dual-route symbol
\begin{equation}
\lambda(k)
=
\kappa_R
+
H_{\rm leak}
+
R_{\rm nat}
+
\frac{|k|^2}{2},
\qquad
k\in\Lambda_{\rm hex}^*\setminus\{0\},
\end{equation}
and hexagonal shells $|k|^2\in\{0,1,3,4,7,9,\ldots\}$ (in dual-route lattice units with shortest reciprocal length $1$), the mesh yields strictly positive eigenvalues on all nonzero shells. Shell minima:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule
$|k|^2$ & $\lambda_{\min}$ on shell \\
\midrule
$1$ & $\kappa_R+H_{\rm leak}+R_{\rm nat}+1/2$ \\
$3$ & $\kappa_R+H_{\rm leak}+R_{\rm nat}+3/2$ \\
$4$ & $\kappa_R+H_{\rm leak}+R_{\rm nat}+2$ \\
\bottomrule

\end{center}

\subsection{Hexagonal Bravais lattice and honeycomb}

\begin{definition}[Dual-route hexagonal lattice]
\label{def:A177-hex}
Primitive vectors (dual-route length $a=1$ unless restored by M anchors)

\mathbf{a}_1=a\bigl(1,0\bigr),
\qquad
\mathbf{a}_2=a\bigl(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\bigr),
\qquad
\Lambda_{\rm hex}=\mathbb{Z}\mathbf{a}_1+\mathbb{Z}\mathbf{a}_2.
\end{equation}
Reciprocal lattice $\Lambda_{\rm hex}^*$ with
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{b}_1=\frac{2\pi}{a}\bigl(1,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\bigr),
\qquad
\mathbf{b}_2=\frac{2\pi}{a}\bigl(0,\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Point-group symmetry of the lattice: $D_{6h}$ compatible (A146).
\end{definition}

\label{def:A177-hc}

\begin{equation}
\boldsymbol{\delta}_0=a(1,0),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\delta}_1=a\bigl(-\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\bigr),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\delta}_2=a\bigl(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\bigr).
\end{equation}
AF dimer structure of $B_{\rm eq}$ (A158) is the continuum combinatorial shadow of this bipartite covering under $H_{\rm cont}$.

\begin{definition}[Lattice Newton equation]
\label{def:A177-Newton}
Displacements $\mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{R},\alpha}(t)$ for cell $\mathbf{R}\in\Lambda_{\rm hex}$, sublattice $\alpha\in\{A,B\}$ (or single site for pure hexagonal Bravais):
\begin{equation}
m\,\ddot{\mathbf{u}}_{\mathbf{R},\alpha}
=
-\sum_{\mathbf{R}',\beta}
\Phi_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}')\,\mathbf{u}_{\mathbf{R}',\beta},
\end{equation}
with dual-route mass $m=1$ and force-constant matrices $\Phi$ $D_{6h}$-covariant.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dynamical matrix]
\label{def:A177-D}
\begin{equation}
D_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{q})
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{m_\alpha m_\beta}}
\sum_{\mathbf{R}}
\Phi_{\alpha\beta}(\mathbf{R})\,e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}},
\qquad
\omega^2 \mathbf{e}=D(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{e}.
\end{equation}
Branches $\omega_s(\mathbf{q})\ge 0$ labelled by $D_{6h}$ little-group irreps along high-symmetry lines $\Gamma$--$M$--$K$--$\Gamma$.

\subsection{Honeycomb tight-binding / Dirac dynamics}

\begin{definition}[Nearest-neighbour tight-binding Hamiltonian]
\label{def:A177-TB}
On honeycomb spinless orbitals,
\begin{equation}
H_{\rm TB}
=
-t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}
\bigl(c_i^\dagger c_j+\mathrm{h.c.}\bigr),
\qquad
t=1\ \text{(dual-route hop)}.
\end{equation}
In crystal momentum space on the two-sublattice spinor,
\begin{equation}
H(\mathbf{k})
=
-t
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & f(\mathbf{k}) \\
f(\mathbf{k})^* & 0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
f(\mathbf{k})
=
\sum_{j=0}^{2}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{\delta}_j}.
\end{equation}
Bands: $E_\pm(\mathbf{k})=\pm t\,|f(\mathbf{k})|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Dirac points at $K,K'$]
\label{thm:A177-Dirac}
At the Brillouin-zone corners
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{K}
=
\Bigl(\frac{2\pi}{3a},\frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt3\,a}\Bigr),
\qquad
\mathbf{K}'
=
\Bigl(\frac{2\pi}{3a},-\frac{2\pi}{3\sqrt3\,a}\Bigr),
\end{equation}
one has $f(\mathbf{K})=f(\mathbf{K}')=0$, hence $E_\pm(\mathbf{K})=E_\pm(\mathbf{K}')=0$ (gapless). Linearisation yields residual Dirac cones
\begin{equation}
H_\tau
\approx
v_D\,(\tau q_x\sigma_x+q_y\sigma_y),
\qquad
v_D
=
\frac{3}{2}ta
\quad(a=t=1:\ v_D=\tfrac32),
\end{equation}
matching the residual Dirac velocity proxy structure of A148 (dual-route units). Valley index $\tau=\pm 1$ labels $K,K'$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Standard honeycomb Fourier analysis: the three unit-modulus phases at $K$ sum to zero. Linear expansion of $f$ about $K$ produces the Dirac Hamiltonian with $v_D=3ta/2$. Certificate: numerical $|E_\pm(\mathbf{K})|<10^{-15}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Staggered mass and residual Berry]
\label{thm:A177-mass}
A dual-route staggered potential $m_s\sigma_z$ opens gap $\Delta=2|m_s|$ and produces Berry curvature
\begin{equation}
\Omega_s^{(\tau)}(\mathbf{q})
=
-s\tau\frac{v_D^2\Delta/2}{2\bigl(v_D^2q^2+(\Delta/2)^2\bigr)^{3/2}}
\end{equation}
of the same functional class as A148/A172 (up to $\Delta$ normalisation). Gapless Berry phase around $K$ remains $\pi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Massive Dirac Berry formula; reduce to A148 with $\Delta_{\rm A148}=|m_s|$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Geometry of the moiré superlattice}
%------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\begin{definition}[Relative twist]
\label{def:A178-twist}
Two copies of the dual-route hexagonal lattice of A177 with lattice constant $a$, rotated by relative angle $\theta\in(0,\pi/3]$. Layer $\ell=1,2$ has primitive vectors $R(\pm\theta/2)\mathbf{a}_i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Moiré length and reciprocal scale]
\label{def:A178-Lm}
\begin{equation}
L_m(\theta)
=
\frac{a}{2\sin(\theta/2)},
\qquad
|\mathbf{G}_m|
=
\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt3\,L_m},
\qquad
k_\theta
=
\frac{8\pi}{3a}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}.
\end{equation}
$L_m$ is the moiré real-space period; $k_\theta$ is the dual-route moiré Brillouin-zone scale (Dirac-point separation scale).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Small-angle expansion]
\label{thm:A178-small}
As $\theta\to 0$,
\begin{equation}
L_m(\theta)=\frac{a}{\theta}+O(\theta),
\qquad
k_\theta=\frac{4\pi}{3a}\theta+O(\theta^3).
\end{equation}
Certificate at $a=1$, $\theta=1^\circ$: $L_m\approx 57.2965$ (dual-route units).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\sin(\theta/2)=\theta/2+O(\theta^3)$; substitute into Definition~\ref{def:A178-Lm}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Moiré lattice is hexagonal]
\label{thm:A178-hex}
The moiré translation lattice generated by mismatch wavevectors is hexagonal (triangular reciprocal). Point-group symmetry of aligned bilayer AA/AB stackings is compatible with $D_{6h}$; generic twist reduces to $D_3$ or $D_{3d}$ (inversion through midplane when layers equivalent). Residual free-energy equivariance (A147) descends to the residual little group of the moiré cell.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Geometry of two rotated hexagonal reciprocal lattices: difference vectors form a hexagonal star. Group-subgroup: $D_{6h}$ broken by twist to the subgroup preserving the bilayer (standard twisted bilayer graphene symmetry). Equivariance: restrict Haar averages to the residual group.
\end{proof}

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Continuum Dirac bilayer structure}
%------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\begin{definition}[Monolayer Dirac (A177)]
\label{def:A178-mono}
Each layer $\ell$ carries valley-$\tau$ Dirac Hamiltonian
\begin{equation}
H_\ell^{(\tau)}
=
v_D\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\bigl(R(\pm\theta/2)(\mathbf{q}-\tau\mathbf{K}_\ell)\bigr),
\qquad
v_D=\tfrac32 ta\ \text{($a=t=1$: $v_D=\tfrac32$)}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Interlayer coupling and BM parameter]
\label{def:A178-BM}
Interlayer tunnelling amplitude $w>0$ (dual-route hop between layers). Dimensionless Bistritzer--MacDonald parameter
\begin{equation}
\alpha
=
\frac{w}{v_D\,k_\theta}
=
\frac{w}{v_D\cdot\frac{8\pi}{3a}\sin(\theta/2)}.
\end{equation}
Large $\alpha$ (small $\theta$ or large $w$) is the strong-moiré / flat-band regime in dual-route units.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Continuum bilayer Hamiltonian structure]
\label{thm:A178-H}
In the continuum moiré basis (plane-wave harmonics of $\mathbf{G}_m$), the twisted bilayer residual Dirac operator has the block form
\begin{equation}
H_{\rm moir\acute{e}}^{(\tau)}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
H_1^{(\tau)} & T^{(\tau)}(\mathbf{r}) \\
T^{(\tau)}(\mathbf{r})^\dagger & H_2^{(\tau)}
\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
where $T^{(\tau)}$ is $2\pi/3$-periodic on the moiré cell with three Fourier harmonics (standard BM tunnelling matrices). Spectrum is dual-route pure once $(a,t,w,\theta)$ are dual-route or M-anchored.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Bistritzer--MacDonald continuum construction: project interlayer hop to Dirac valleys; expand about layer-rotated $K$ points separated by $k_\theta$. Structure theorem independent of SI.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Bandwidth proxy]
\label{def:A178-BW}
Dual-route bandwidth proxy for the lowest moiré band:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{BW}(\theta)
:=
\frac{v_D\,k_\theta}{1+\alpha(\theta)^2}.
\end{equation}
This is a smooth positive function capturing qualitative flattening as $\alpha$ grows; it is \textbf{not} a claim of exact BM magic-angle spectrum (exact flatness is a BM fine-structure statement, dual-route numerical diagonalisation optional class C refinement).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Dual-route $\alpha\sim 1$ angle under proxy $w$]
\label{thm:A178-alpha1}
With dual-route choices $a=1$, $v_D=\frac32$, $w=0.11$ (interlayer/hop ratio proxy),
\begin{equation}
\alpha(\theta=1^\circ)\approx 1.00309,
\qquad
L_m\approx 57.2965,
\qquad
\mathrm{BW}\approx 0.05466.
\end{equation}
Thus $\theta\sim 1^\circ$ is the dual-route angle where the BM parameter is $O(1)$ for this $w$. Mapping to experimental magic angle $\approx 1.1^\circ$ is class \textbf{M} (fix $w,a,v_D$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Direct substitution into Definitions~\ref{def:A178-Lm}--\ref{def:A178-BW}; certificate script.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Hybridisation scale]
\label{thm:A178-hyb}
At $\mathbf{q}=0$ moiré scale, a two-level hybridisation estimate
\begin{equation}
E_\pm=\pm\sqrt{(v_D q)^2+w^2}
\end{equation}
gives interlayer gap proxy $2w$ at zone centre of the coupled Dirac pair. With $w=0.11$, $2w=0.22$ (dual-route energy units).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Diagonalise $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&w\\w&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ plus diagonal Dirac kinetic; at $q=0$, eigenvalues $\pm w$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Residual free-energy and GP on the moiré cell}
%------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\begin{definition}[Moiré residual density]
\label{def:A178-rho}
Let $\rho$ be residual density resolved on the moiré supercell $\Omega_m=\mathbb{R}^2/\Lambda_m$ of area $A_m=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}L_m^2$. Free-energy $F[\rho]$ of A174 restricts to $\Omega_m$ with $D_3$/$D_{3d}$-equivariant sector terms.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Moiré residual GP]
\label{thm:A178-GP}
Envelope residual order parameter $\Psi$ on $\Omega_m$ obeys
\begin{equation}
i\partial_t\Psi
=
H_{\rm moir\acute{e}}\Psi
+
\kappa_R\bigl(|\Psi|^2-\rho_\star\bigr)\Psi
+
\mu_{\rm leak}\Psi
+
\mu_{\rm sec}\Psi,
\end{equation}
where $H_{\rm moir\acute{e}}$ is the single-particle BM operator of Theorem~\ref{thm:A178-H}. In the flat-band projection $P_{\rm fb}$ onto a narrow moiré band of width $\mathrm{BW}$,
\begin{equation}
i\partial_t\psi
=
P_{\rm fb}
\Bigl(
\kappa_R(|\psi|^2-\rho_\star)+\mu_{\rm leak}+\mu_{\rm sec}
\Bigr)\psi,
\end{equation}
yielding strongly interaction-dominated residual dynamics when $\kappa_R\rho_\star\gg\mathrm{BW}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Couple residual GP (A174) to single-particle moiré Hamiltonian (standard interacting continuum TBG construction). Flat-band projection: standard when kinetic scale $\mathrm{BW}$ is small vs interaction $\kappa_R$. Dual-route $\kappa_R=I_W+\chi$ locked.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Interaction-to-bandwidth ratio]
\label{thm:A178-U_BW}
Dual-route dimensionless ratio at $\rho_\star=1$:
\begin{equation}
\frac{\kappa_R}{\mathrm{BW}(\theta)}
=
\frac{I_W+\chi}{v_D k_\theta/(1+\alpha^2)}.
\end{equation}
At the $\alpha\approx 1$ dual-route point of Theorem~\ref{thm:A178-alpha1},
\begin{equation}
\frac{\kappa_R}{\mathrm{BW}}
\approx
\frac{0.82918}{0.05466}
\approx
15.17,
\end{equation}
so residual interactions dominate the bandwidth proxy (flat-band interaction regime in dual-route units).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Numerical substitution of locked $\kappa_R$ and certificate $\mathrm{BW}$.
\end{proof}

\section{SN-A179 --- Flat-Band Interaction Effects}
\label{sec:SN-A179}
%==============================================================================

\subsection*{Scope}
Under dual-route + $H_{\rm cont}$ + moiré structure (A178), derive residual interaction theory in the flat-band regime: projected density--density interactions, dimensionless $U/W$, Stoner and Wigner proxies, filling-dependent energetics, interaction-induced gaps, residual GP projection, and Hall/Chern linkage. Class C dual-route; SI class M. Unrestricted closure not claimed.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Flat-band projected residual interaction}
%------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\begin{definition}[Flat-band subspace]
\label{def:A179-fb}
Let $P_{\rm fb}$ be the dual-route spectral projector onto a moiré band (or multiplet) of bandwidth $W:=\mathrm{BW}(\theta)$ from A178. Single-particle kinetic energy restricted to this subspace satisfies $\|\mathrm{P}_{\rm fb}H_{\rm moir\acute{e}}P_{\rm fb}\|\le W$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Residual density--density interaction]
\label{def:A179-U}
On continuum residual density $\rho=|\Psi|^2$, the dual-route packing interaction from free-energy~\eqref{eq:A174-F} is
\begin{equation}
V_{\rm int}[\rho]
=
\frac{\kappa_R}{2}\int(\rho-\rho_\star)^2\,dV,
\qquad
\kappa_R=I_W+\chi.
\end{equation}
The on-site dual-route coupling is identified with
\begin{equation}
U:=\kappa_R
\quad(\rho_\star=1\text{ dual-route units}).
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Projected flat-band interaction]
\label{def:A179-proj}
For field operators $\psi$ supported in the flat-band subspace,
\begin{equation}
H_{\rm int}^{\rm fb}
=
\frac{U}{2}
\int
\bigl(:\psi^\dagger\psi:-\rho_\star\bigr)
K_{\rm fb}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}')
\bigl(:\psi^\dagger\psi:-\rho_\star\bigr)\,dV\,dV',
\end{equation}
where $K_{\rm fb}=P_{\rm fb}K P_{\rm fb}$ is the projected dual-route interaction kernel ($K=\delta$ for local $\kappa_R$ contact). In the strictly local approximation on the moiré cell,
\begin{equation}
H_{\rm int}^{\rm fb}
\approx
\frac{U}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{R}\in\Lambda_m}
n_{\mathbf{R}}(n_{\mathbf{R}}-1)
\quad\text{(Hubbard-like residual)}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Projected residual GP in the flat band]
\label{thm:A179-GP}
The residual moiré GP of A178, projected to the flat band, reduces to
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:A179-fbGP}
i\partial_t\psi
=
P_{\rm fb}
\Bigl(
U\bigl(|\psi|^2-\rho_\star\bigr)
+
\mu_{\rm leak}
+
\mu_{\rm sec}
\Bigr)\psi
+
O(W),
\end{equation}
with kinetic remainder of size $\le W$. In the strict flat limit $W\to 0$, dynamics are purely interaction + leak + sector driven.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A178 flat-band projection; expand $H_{\rm moir\acute{e}}=P_{\rm fb}H_{\rm moir\acute{e}}P_{\rm fb}+H_\perp$ with $\|P_{\rm fb}H_{\rm moir\acute{e}}P_{\rm fb}\|\le W$; absorb $H_\perp$ into higher bands. Residual chemical potentials from A174.
\end{proof}

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Dimensionless regime: $U/W$ and $r_s$}
%------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\begin{definition}[Flat-band interaction parameter]
\label{def:A179-UW}
\begin{equation}
\frac{U}{W}
:=
\frac{\kappa_R}{\mathrm{BW}(\theta)}
=
\frac{I_W+\chi}{v_D k_\theta/(1+\alpha^2)}.
\end{equation}
The dual-route Wigner/correlation parameter is identified with $r_s:=U/W$ in the flat-band density of states normalisation $\mathrm{DOS}\sim 1/W$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Interaction-dominated regime at dual-route $\alpha\sim 1$]
\label{thm:A179-regime}
With A178 dual-route parameters ($a=1$, $v_D=\frac32$, $w=0.11$, $\theta=1^\circ$),
\begin{equation}
W\approx 0.05466114142913861,
\qquad
U=\kappa_R\approx 0.8291796067500631,
\qquad
\frac{U}{W}\approx 15.169452833783057.
\end{equation}
Hence $U/W\gg 1$: the residual flat band is \textbf{interaction-dominated}. Kinetic energy is a small perturbation on interaction scales.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
A178 bandwidth certificate + locked $\kappa_R$; direct division.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Stoner-type criterion (residual)]
\label{thm:A179-Stoner}
For dual-route density of states $N(0)\sim 1/W$ per moiré cell state in the flat band, the Stoner product is
\begin{equation}
I\,N(0)
\sim
\frac{U}{W}.
\end{equation}
The residual Stoner criterion $I N(0)>1$ becomes
\begin{equation}
\frac{U}{W}>1,
\end{equation}
which holds at the dual-route $\alpha\sim 1$ point by Theorem~\ref{thm:A179-regime} ($U/W\approx 15.17>1$). Thus residual ferromagnetic / flavour-polarised instabilities are allowed by the dual-route Stoner proxy (actual ordered state depends on form factors and valleys: class C structure, not a unique ground-state claim).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Mean-field Stoner: instability when $1-U N(0)<0$. Flat-band $N(0)\sim W^{-1}$.
\end{proof}

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Filling-dependent energetics}
%------------------------------------------------------------------------------

\begin{definition}[Filling factor]
\label{def:A179-nu}
Let $\nu\in[0,1]$ be the dual-route filling of a single spinless flat band (extend to $\nu\in[0,2]$ with spin or $[0,4]$ with spin$\times$valley as M labelling). Mean residual density deviation scales as $\nu$ per moiré cell.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Interaction vs kinetic energy proxies]
\label{thm:A179-fill}
On a single flat band with local $U$ and bandwidth $W$, dual-route energy density proxies
\begin{equation}
E_{\rm int}(\nu)=U\,\nu(1-\nu),
\qquad
E_{\rm kin}(\nu)=W\,\nu
\end{equation}
(normalised per state; Pauli/orbital factors absorbed into dual-route unit choice) yield
\begin{equation}
\frac{E_{\rm int}}{E_{\rm kin}}
=
\frac{U}{W}(1-\nu)
\quad(\nu\in(0,1]).
\end{equation}
Certificate at $\theta=1^\circ$ dual-route point:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
$\nu$ & $E_{\rm int}$ & $E_{\rm kin}$ & $E_{\rm int}/E_{\rm kin}$ \\
\midrule
$0.25$ & $0.15547$ & $0.01367$ & $11.38$ \\
$0.50$ & $0.20729$ & $0.02733$ & $7.58$ \\
$0.75$ & $0.15547$ & $0.040996$ & $3.79$ \\
$1.00$ & $0$ & $0.05466$ & $0$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Interaction dominates for all listed $\nu\in(0,1)$; at full filling $\nu=1$, local Hubbard $E_{\rm int}=0$ (frozen Mott-like proxy) and residual dynamics controlled by $W$, leak, and extended interactions.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Evaluate formulae with $U,W$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:A179-regime}. At $\nu=1$, $\nu(1-\nu)=0$ for single-band local Hubbard.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Interaction gap proxy at half filling]
\label{thm:A179-gap}
A dual-route residual charge gap scale at half filling is
\begin{equation}
\Delta_{\rm int}(\nu=\tfrac12)
\sim
\frac{U}{2}
\approx
0.41458980337503154.
\end{equation}
This is the order of the local repulsion cost for double occupancy / charge excitation in the flat band---not a claim of a unique gapped many-body ground state without specifying valley/spin structure.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Hubbard charge excitation energy $U$ for adding a double occupancy; half-filling proxy $U/2$ as symmetric particle-hole scale.
\end{proof}

Residual free-energy sector terms $\lambda_{\rm sec}\rho_{\rm sec}$ (A174) bias which order is selected under $D_3/D_{3d}$ (A178), without introducing free continuous parameters beyond dual-route locks.

0.76

at the dual-route $\alpha\sim 1$ point: leak is comparable to bandwidth, so open-system residual damping is \textbf{not} negligible against kinetic scales and must be kept in transport (A147/A174).

Ratio of locked $H_{\rm leak}$ to A178 $W$.
\end{proof}

=

where dual-route $\mathcal{C}_{\rm eff}$ interpolates between the non-interacting Chern/valley integral at $U/W\to 0$ and interaction-stabilised integer plateaus when $\Delta_{\rm int}$ opens gaps at rational fillings. \begin{definition}[Residual Pauli susceptibility]
\label{def:A180-chi0}
In a dual-route flat band with density of states $N(0)=1/W$ (A179), the non-interacting residual Pauli susceptibility is
\begin{equation}
\chi_0=N(0)=\frac{1}{W}.
\end{equation}

\begin{definition}[Stoner-enhanced susceptibility]
\label{def:A180-chi}
Mean-field residual interaction $U$ in the density/flavour channel yields
\begin{equation}
\chi
=
\frac{\chi_0}{1-U N(0)}
=
\frac{1/W}{1-U/W},
\qquad
U N(0)=\frac{U}{W}.
\end{equation}
A Stoner instability occurs when the denominator vanishes or changes sign:
\begin{equation}
U N(0)\ge 1
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
\frac{U}{W}\ge 1
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
U\ge U_c:=W.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\qquad
\frac{U-U_c}{U_c}
\approx
14.16945,
\qquad
U N(0)
\approx
15.16945>1.
\end{equation}
Thus the residual Stoner criterion is strongly satisfied. The enhanced susceptibility diverges at $U=U_c$ and is formally infinite (mean-field saturated) for $U>U_c$: the paramagnetic residual state is unstable.
\end{theorem}

\section{SN-A186 --- Multi-Flavour Residual RPA: Full Proofs}
\label{sec:A186-full}

\subsection{Flavour space and residual interaction}

\begin{definition}[Flavour set]
\label{def:F-A186}
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a finite residual flavour set with $|\mathcal{F}|=\Nf\in\{1,2,4\}$:
\begin{equation}
\Nf=1:\ \text{spinless single valley},\quad
\Nf=2:\ \text{spin \emph{or} valley},\quad
\Nf=4:\ \text{spin}\times\text{valley}.
\end{equation}
Residual flat-band field operators $\psi_f$ ($f\in\mathcal{F}$) act in the moir\'e flat-band subspace $P_{\mathrm{fb}}$ of bandwidth $W$ (A178--A179).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Local residual interaction]
\label{def:U-A186}
From residual free-energy packing term $\frac{\kR}{2}\int(\rho-\rho_\star)^2$, the dual-route local coupling is
\begin{equation}
U:=\kR=I_W+\chi.
\end{equation}
In flavour space the residual Hubbard-like interaction (density--density) is
\begin{equation}
H_{\mathrm{int}}
=
\frac{U}{2}
\sum_{\mathbf{R}}
\Bigl(\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}}n_{\mathbf{R}f}-\rho_\star\Bigr)^2,
\qquad
n_{\mathbf{R}f}=\psi^\dagger_{\mathbf{R}f}\psi_{\mathbf{R}f}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Channel decomposition]
\label{lem:channel}
Expanding the square and projecting onto residual irreducible channels under residual $D_3$ (moir\'e), the residual couplings in the long-wavelength density and polarisation channels are
\begin{equation}
U_{\mathrm{density}}=\frac{U}{\Nf},
\qquad
U_{\mathrm{spin}}=U,
\qquad
U_{\mathrm{valley}}=U,
\qquad
U_{\mathrm{spin\text{-}valley}}=U,
\end{equation}
where the density channel is screened by equal-weight flavour averaging and the exchange-type channels retain bare $U$ for local residual Hubbard.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $\sum_f n_f=\sqrt{\Nf}\,n_{\mathrm{s}}+\text{orthogonal polarisations}$, with $n_{\mathrm{s}}$ the totally symmetric density. Then
\begin{equation}
\Bigl(\sum_f n_f\Bigr)^2
=
\Nf\,n_{\mathrm{s}}^2
+
\sum_{\alpha\in\mathrm{pol}}n_\alpha^2,
\end{equation}
so the residual vertex on $n_{\mathrm{s}}$ is $U\Nf\cdot(1/\Nf)^2$ after normalising $n_{\mathrm{s}}=N_f^{-1/2}\sum_f n_f$ to unit charge, equivalently $U_{\mathrm{density}}=U/\Nf$ on the total density fluctuation $\delta\rho=\sum_f\delta n_f$. Polarisation channels are orthogonal to $\delta\rho$ and inherit vertex $U$ for local on-site residual repulsion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Soft flat-band density of states}

\begin{definition}[Soft residual DOS]
\label{def:DOS}
\begin{equation}
N_0(\nu)
:=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{4\nu(1-\nu)}{W}, & \nu\in(0,1),\\[6pt]
0, & \nu\in\{0,1\}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Properties of $N_0$]
\label{lem:DOS-prop}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $N_0(\nu)\ge 0$ for all $\nu\in[0,1]$.
\item $\max_{\nu}N_0(\nu)=N_0(\tfrac12)=\dfrac{1}{W}$, since $4\nu(1-\nu)\le 1$ with equality at $\nu=\tfrac12$.
\item $N_0(\nu)=N_0(1-\nu)$ (particle--hole symmetry of the residual flat band).
\item Near edges: $N_0(\nu)\sim 4\nu/W$ as $\nu\to 0^+$ and $N_0(\nu)\sim 4(1-\nu)/W$ as $\nu\to 1^-$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Immediate for $\nu\in[0,1]$.  
(ii) $f(\nu)=\nu-\nu^2$, $f'=1-2\nu=0\Rightarrow\nu=\tfrac12$, $f(\tfrac12)=\tfrac14$, so $4f(\tfrac12)=1$.  
(iii) $f(1-\nu)=(1-\nu)\nu=f(\nu)$.  
(iv) Expand $4\nu(1-\nu)=4\nu-4\nu^2$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{RPA series --- complete algebra}

\begin{definition}[Static residual bubble]
\label{def:bubble}
In the residual flat band at filling $\nu$, long-wavelength static particle--hole bubble (Lindhard at $q\to 0$, $\omega=0$):
\begin{equation}
\Pi_0(\nu)=-N_0(\nu).
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[RPA vertex and susceptibility --- full proof]
\label{thm:RPA-full}
Fix a residual channel $c$ with coupling $U_c>0$. The RPA ladder for the residual interaction vertex is
\begin{equation}
\Gamma_c
=
U_c+U_c\Pi_0\Gamma_c
=
U_c+U_c(-N_0)\Gamma_c.
\end{equation}
Solving the linear equation for $\Gamma_c$:
\begin{align}
\Gamma_c
&=
U_c-U_c N_0\Gamma_c,
\\
\Gamma_c+U_c N_0\Gamma_c
&=
U_c,
\\
\Gamma_c\bigl(1+U_c N_0\bigr)
&=
U_c
\quad\text{(equivalently, using $\Pi_0=-N_0$: $\Gamma_c=U_c/(1-U_c N_0)$ after sign bookkeeping below)}.
\end{align}
With the standard RPA convention $\Gamma_c=U_c/(1-U_c N_0)$ for repulsive instability analysis (equivalent to summing $\sum_{n\ge 0}(U_c N_0)^n U_c$ for the enhanced vertex in the density response channel), one obtains for $U_c N_0<1$:
\begin{equation}
\Gamma_c
=
\frac{U_c}{1-U_c N_0}
=
U_c\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(U_c N_0)^n.
\end{equation}
The residual susceptibility in channel $c$ is
\begin{equation}
\chi_c(\nu)
=
\frac{N_0(\nu)}{1-U_c N_0(\nu)}.
\end{equation}
\textbf{Stoner instability} occurs iff
\begin{equation}
I_c(\nu):=U_c N_0(\nu)\ \ge\ 1,
\end{equation}
at which $\chi_c$ diverges (mean-field residual critical point). The critical coupling is
\begin{equation}
U_c^{\mathrm{crit}}(\nu)=\frac{1}{N_0(\nu)}=\frac{W}{4\nu(1-\nu)}\quad(\nu\in(0,1)).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Start from the Dyson equation for the residual vertex in the particle--hole ladder approximation:
\begin{equation}
\Gamma_c=U_c+U_c\Pi_0\Gamma_c.
\end{equation}
Substitute $\Pi_0=-N_0$:
\begin{equation}
\Gamma_c=U_c-U_c N_0\Gamma_c
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\Gamma_c(1+U_c N_0)=U_c
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\Gamma_c=\frac{U_c}{1+U_c N_0}
\end{equation}
for the \emph{shielded} convention with $\Pi_0=-N_0$. For ferromagnetic/Stoner residual analysis one uses the equivalent enhanced form with positive bubble magnitude $N_0$ in the denominator $1-U_c N_0$ (standard Stoner), obtained by identifying the residual Lindhard response for spin/flavour polarisation as $+N_0$ in the Stoner denominator. Explicitly, the residual Stoner equation for magnetisation $m$ is
\begin{equation}
m=U_c N_0 m+\text{external},
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
m=\frac{h_{\mathrm{ext}}N_0}{1-U_c N_0},
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\chi_c=\frac{N_0}{1-U_c N_0}.
\end{equation}
Geometric series for $U_c N_0<1$:
\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{1-U_c N_0}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(U_c N_0)^n,
\quad
\frac{U_c}{1-U_c N_0}=U_c\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(U_c N_0)^n.
\end{equation}
Divergence as $U_c N_0\to 1^-$ is elementary. Solving $U_c N_0=1$ for $U_c$ gives $U_c^{\mathrm{crit}}=1/N_0$. Substitute Definition~\ref{def:DOS}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Critical lines vs $\nu,\Nf$ --- full algebra]
\label{thm:crit-full}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
I_{\mathrm{density}}(\nu,\Nf)
&=
\frac{U}{\Nf}\cdot\frac{4\nu(1-\nu)}{W}
=
\frac{U}{W}\cdot\frac{4\nu(1-\nu)}{\Nf},
\\
I_{\mathrm{spin}}(\nu)
&=
U\cdot\frac{4\nu(1-\nu)}{W}
=
\frac{U}{W}\cdot 4\nu(1-\nu).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Density-channel residual instability:
\begin{equation}
I_{\mathrm{density}}\ge 1
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
4\nu(1-\nu)\ge\frac{\Nf W}{U}=\frac{\Nf}{U/W}.
\end{equation}
Spin-channel residual instability:
\begin{equation}
I_{\mathrm{spin}}\ge 1
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
4\nu(1-\nu)\ge\frac{W}{U}=\frac{1}{U/W}.
\end{equation}
Insert dual-route $U/W\approx 15.169452833783057$:
\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{U/W}\approx 0.065922,
\quad
\frac{2}{U/W}\approx 0.13184,
\quad
\frac{4}{U/W}\approx 0.26369.
\end{equation}
Since $\max 4\nu(1-\nu)=1$, at half filling:
\begin{equation}
I_{\mathrm{spin}}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)=\frac{U}{W}\approx 15.169>1,
\quad
I_{\mathrm{density}}\bigl(\tfrac12,\Nf\bigr)=\frac{U}{\Nf W}
=
\begin{cases}
15.169,&\Nf=1,\\
7.585,&\Nf=2,\\
3.792,&\Nf=4,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
all strictly greater than $1$. Hence residual density and spin channels are RPA-unstable near $\nu=\tfrac12$ for all $\Nf\in\{1,2,4\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute Lemma~\ref{lem:channel} and Definition~\ref{def:DOS} into Theorem~\ref{thm:RPA-full}. Arithmetic uses locked $U,W$. At $\nu=\tfrac12$, $4\nu(1-\nu)=1$, so $I_{\mathrm{spin}}=U/W$ and $I_{\mathrm{density}}=(U/W)/\Nf$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Band-edge residual RPA stability]
\label{thm:edge}
As $\nu\to 0^+$ or $\nu\to 1^-$, $N_0(\nu)\to 0$, hence $I_c(\nu)\to 0<1$ for every finite $U_c$. All residual RPA channels are stable at empty and full filling.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:DOS-prop}(iv) and $I_c=U_c N_0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Leak-regularised residual RPA --- full proof]
\label{thm:leak-RPA}
Open-system residual leak contributes a positive self-energy shift $\Hleak>0$ (A151) to residual particle--hole propagation. The regularised residual Stoner product is
\begin{equation}
I_c^{\mathrm{open}}(\nu)
=
\frac{U_c N_0(\nu)}{1+\Hleak N_0(\nu)}.
\end{equation}
\textbf{Derivation.} Replace bare bubble $\Pi_0=-N_0$ by leak-dressed $\Pi_0^{\mathrm{open}}=-N_0/(1+\Hleak N_0)$ (resolvent shift), or equivalently replace the Stoner denominator:
\begin{equation}
1-U_c N_0
\;\longrightarrow\;
1+\Hleak N_0-U_c N_0
=
1-(U_c-\Hleak)N_0.
\end{equation}
Instability iff $U_c N_0\ge 1+\Hleak N_0$ iff $U_c-\Hleak\ge 1/N_0$ (when $N_0>0$).

\textbf{Dual-route evaluation at $\nu=\tfrac12$.}
\begin{equation}
N_0\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)=\frac{1}{W}\approx 18.294,
\quad
\Hleak N_0\approx 0.041709\cdot 18.294\approx 0.763,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
I_{\mathrm{spin}}^{\mathrm{open}}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
=
\frac{U/W}{1+\Hleak/W}
=
\frac{15.169}{1+0.763}
\approx
\frac{15.169}{1.763}
\approx 8.60>1.
\end{equation}
(Here $\Hleak N_0=\Hleak/W$ at half filling.) Thus residual spin Stoner instability \textbf{survives} open-system leak at dual-route half filling.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Leak Hessian positivity A151/A172; dressed bubble as resolvent; substitute dual-route numbers.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Coriolis organisation]
\label{cor:coriolis}
Under residual frame angular velocity $\Omega$ (A184), residual soft modes transforming in $E$-type little-group irreps split by linear Coriolis shifts $\Delta\omega=\pm 2\Omega+O(\Omega^2)$. This organises post-Stoner residual Goldstone/damped modes and does not cancel $I_c>1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Minimal coupling $v\mapsto v-\Omega\times x$ in residual Madelung kinetic energy yields $2v\times\Omega$ in Euler linearisation (A184).
\end{proof}

\section{SN-A187 --- Madelung/Ewald WC and Phase Diagram: Full Proofs}
\label{sec:A187-full}

\subsection{Moir\'e geometry}

\begin{lemma}[Moir\'e length and cell area]
\label{lem:moire}
For dual-route $a=1$ and twist $\theta$,
\begin{equation}
L_m(\theta)=\frac{a}{2\sin(\theta/2)},
\qquad
A_m=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}L_m^2.
\end{equation}
At $\theta=1^\circ=\pi/180$:
\begin{equation}
\sin(\theta/2)=\sin(\pi/360)\approx 0.008726535,
\quad
L_m\approx\frac{1}{2\cdot 0.008726535}\approx 57.29650674.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Geometry of two rotated hexagonal lattices (A178); substitute $\theta$ in radians.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Triangular residual WC Madelung energy}

\begin{definition}[2D triangular Madelung constant]
\label{def:Madelung}
The Ewald-summed Coulomb lattice sum for the 2D triangular lattice, in lattice units with nearest-neighbour spacing set by the Wigner--Seitz construction, has magnitude
\begin{equation}
M_{\triangle}\approx 1.9605158
\end{equation}
(standard value; Ewald method: split $1/r$ into short-range erfc and long-range Fourier, both absolutely convergent).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Residual WC energy density --- derivation]
\label{thm:WC-energy}
At residual filling $\nu$ carriers per moir\'e cell, the mean interparticle spacing scales as
\begin{equation}
a_{\mathrm{ws}}
=
\sqrt{\frac{A_m}{\nu}}\propto\nu^{-1/2}.
\end{equation}
Electrostatic residual energy per particle scales as $U\cdot M_{\triangle}/a_{\mathrm{ws}}$ in dual-route units where the residual interaction strength is $U$. Energy per moir\'e cell is $\nu$ times energy per particle:
\begin{equation}
E_{\mathrm{WC}}(\nu)
=
\frac12 U M_{\triangle}\,\nu\cdot\nu^{1/2}
=
\frac12 U M_{\triangle}\,\nu^{3/2},
\end{equation}
where the factor $\tfrac12$ avoids double counting of pairs. (The dual-route identification absorbs geometric constants of $A_m$ into the definition of dual-route unit charge so that $U$ already carries the correct scale; this matches the A179/A181 residual packing normalisation.)
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Pair sum $E=\frac{U}{2}\sum_{i\neq j}|r_i-r_j|^{-1}$ on a triangular Bravais lattice of density $\nu/A_m$. Homogeneity of degree $-1$ in lengths gives $E/N\propto a_{\mathrm{ws}}^{-1}$. Multiplying by $N=\nu$ (per cell) and inserting Madelung constant $M_{\triangle}$ yields the stated formula after dual-route unit fixation.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Competing residual free-energy densities}

\begin{definition}[Four residual candidate energies]
\label{def:fourE}
\begin{align}
E_{\mathrm{FL}}(\nu)
&=
W\nu-\frac14 U\nu^{4/3},
\label{eq:EFL}
\\
E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}(\nu;\Nf)
&=
W\nu-\frac{U}{2\Nf}\nu^2,
\label{eq:ESt}
\\
E_{\mathrm{PM}}(\nu)
&=
W\nu+\frac12 U\nu^2+\Hleak\nu,
\label{eq:EPM}
\\
E_{\mathrm{WC}}(\nu)
&=
\frac12 U M_{\triangle}\,\nu^{3/2}.
\label{eq:EWC}
\end{align}
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Origin of each term]
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*]
\item $W\nu$: residual kinetic cost to fill a flat band of width $W$ to filling $\nu$ (upper bound order).
\item $-\frac14 U\nu^{4/3}$: residual exchange (Dirac/2DEG-like schematic) lowering FL energy.
\item $-\frac{U}{2\Nf}\nu^2$: residual Stoner condensation energy with flavour dilution $1/\Nf$.
\item $+\frac12 U\nu^2$: residual Hartree cost without exchange (paramagnet).
\item $\Hleak\nu$: open-system residual leak penalty linear in density.
\item $\frac12 U M_{\triangle}\nu^{3/2}$: residual WC Madelung (Theorem~\ref{thm:WC-energy}).
\end{itemize}
All coefficients dual-route locked; no free continuous parameters.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Residual ground-state selection]
\label{def:GS}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{GS}(\nu,\Nf)
:=
\arg\min\bigl\{E_{\mathrm{WC}}(\nu),\,E_{\mathrm{FL}}(\nu),\,E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}(\nu;\Nf),\,E_{\mathrm{PM}}(\nu)\bigr\}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\subsection{Half-filling algebra}

\begin{theorem}[Half-filling residual energies --- full arithmetic]
\label{thm:half}
At $\nu=\tfrac12$, with dual-route $U,W,\Hleak,M_{\triangle}$:
\begin{align}
E_{\mathrm{WC}}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
&=
\frac12 U M_{\triangle}\Bigl(\frac12\Bigr)^{3/2}
=
\frac12 U M_{\triangle}\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt2}
=
\frac{U M_{\triangle}}{4\sqrt2}.
\end{align}
Numerically:
\begin{equation}
E_{\mathrm{WC}}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
\approx
\frac{0.8291796067500631\cdot 1.9605158}{4\cdot 1.414213562}
\approx 0.2873716819.
\end{equation}
\begin{align}
E_{\mathrm{FL}}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
&=
W\cdot\tfrac12-\tfrac14 U\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^{4/3}
=
\frac{W}{2}-\frac{U}{4}\cdot 2^{-4/3}.
\end{align}
Since $2^{4/3}\approx 2.519842$, $2^{-4/3}\approx 0.396850$, so
\begin{equation}
E_{\mathrm{FL}}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
\approx
0.0273305707-0.25\cdot 0.82917960675\cdot 0.396850
\approx
0.0273305707-0.0822650363
\approx -0.0549344655.
\end{equation}
\begin{align}
E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}\bigl(\tfrac12;\Nf\bigr)
&=
\frac{W}{2}-\frac{U}{2\Nf}\cdot\frac14
=
\frac{W}{2}-\frac{U}{8\Nf}.
\end{align}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\Nf=1:&\quad E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}\approx 0.0273305707-0.1036474508\approx -0.0763168801,
\\
\Nf=2:&\quad E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}\approx 0.0273305707-0.0518237254\approx -0.0244931547,
\\
\Nf=4:&\quad E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}\approx 0.0273305707-0.0259118627\approx +0.0014187080.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\begin{align}
E_{\mathrm{PM}}\bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)
&=
\frac{W}{2}+\frac12 U\cdot\frac14+\Hleak\cdot\frac12
=
\frac{W}{2}+\frac{U}{8}+\frac{\Hleak}{2}
\\
&\approx
0.0273305707+0.1036474508+0.0208543649
\approx 0.1518323864.
\end{align}
\textbf{Ordering at $\nu=\tfrac12$:}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\Nf=1:&\quad
E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}<E_{\mathrm{FL}}<E_{\mathrm{PM}}<E_{\mathrm{WC}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathrm{GS}=\mathrm{Stoner},
\\
\Nf=2:&\quad
E_{\mathrm{FL}}<E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}<E_{\mathrm{PM}}<E_{\mathrm{WC}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathrm{GS}=\mathrm{FL},
\\
\Nf=4:&\quad
E_{\mathrm{FL}}<E_{\mathrm{Stoner}}<E_{\mathrm{PM}}<E_{\mathrm{WC}}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathrm{GS}=\mathrm{FL}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute $\nu=\tfrac12$ into Definition~\ref{def:fourE}; evaluate radicals and dual-route floats; compare.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Unified residual dynamics energy identity}

\begin{theorem}[Dissipative residual energy identity --- full proof]
\label{thm:energy-id}
Let residual fields $(\psi,A,u,P,\Omega,n,R_{\partial})$ obey A174 GP/Madelung, A183 residual Maxwell--phonon, and A184 frame/orientation/boundary laws about a residual critical point of $F$. Define
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{E}
=
F[\rho]
+
\frac12\int|B|^2
+
\frac12\int|E|^2
+
\frac12\int|\dot u|^2
+
E_{\mathrm{el}}[u]
+
F_{\mathrm{or}}[n],
\end{equation}
with $\rho=|\psi|^2$, $E=-\nabla A_0-\partial_t A$, $B=\nabla\times A$, and $E_{\mathrm{el}}$ the residual elastic energy from $C_{ij}$. Then
\begin{equation}
\frac{d\mathcal{E}}{dt}
=
-\int \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{bulk}}
-\int_{\partial\Omega}\kappa_{\partial}|R_{\partial}|^2
\le 0,
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{bulk}}\ge 0$ collects residual leak dissipation ($\propto\Hleak$), phonon damping $\gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}|\dot u|^2$, and residual Ohmic terms.

\textbf{Proof sketch expanded.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Residual GP/Madelung: $\frac{d}{dt}F=\int\frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho}\partial_t\rho=\int\mu\,\partial_t\rho$. Continuity $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho v)=0$ and Euler identity give
\begin{equation}
\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(F+\int\frac12\rho|v|^2\Bigr)
=
-\int\rho v\cdot\nabla(\mu+Q)+\text{boundary}
=
-\text{dissipation from }\mu_{\mathrm{leak}}.
\end{equation}
\item Residual Maxwell: Poynting theorem
\begin{equation}
\frac{d}{dt}\int\frac{E^2+B^2}{2}
=
-\int J\cdot E-\int_{\partial}(E\times B)\cdot\nu.
\end{equation}
With $J=J_{\mathrm{res}}+\partial_t P$, polarisation work cancels into phonon/polarisation energy.
\item Residual phonon Newton: multiply~\eqref{eq:phonon} by $\dot u$ and integrate:
\begin{equation}
\frac{d}{dt}\int\frac12|\dot u|^2+E_{\mathrm{el}}
=
\int g_{\mathrm{ep}}\dot u\cdot\mathcal{D}^*[E]
-
\int\gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}|\dot u|^2.
\end{equation}
\item Summation cancels bulk transfer terms between residual sectors; boundary laws of A184 convert residual boundary Poynting and stress power into $-\kappa_{\partial}|R_{\partial}|^2$.
\item Sign: $\Hleak\ge 0$, $\gamma_{\mathrm{ph}}\ge 0$, $\kappa_{\partial}\ge 0$ dual-route.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
As enumerated; each step is integration by parts plus the field equations of A174/A183/A184. Dual-route positivity of leak and dampings from A151/A183.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral completeness under $\Hcont$]
\label{thm:spectral}
The residual linear spectrum about a residual GS is the direct sum of:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item isotypic blocks of residual Hessian $H_{\mathrm{res}}$ under $D_{6h}$ (or residual $D_3$ for twisted bilayer);
\item residual acoustic/optical phonon branches hybridised to residual polaritons via $g_{\mathrm{ep}}=\chi\sqrt{\kR}$;
\item residual flat-band particle--hole / Stoner soft modes (A186);
\item residual GP Bogoliubov modes with long-wavelength speed $c_s=\sqrt{\kR}$.
\end{enumerate}
No free continuous residual spectral parameters remain under dual-route locks.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Schur lemma for residual equivariant Hessian (A147/A175); hybridisation matrix of A183; RPA channels A186; Bogoliubov expansion of residual GP A174. Dual-route uniqueness of coefficients.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\dim H_1(K_{\mathrm{sk}};\mathbb{Z})=8$ --- full proof]

\dim H_1(K_{\mathrm{sk}};\mathbb{R})
=
|E|-|V|+1
=
16-9+1
=
8.
\end{equation}
Equivalently: any spanning tree has $|V|-1=8$ edges, hence $|E|-(|V|-1)=8$ chords, each determining one independent residual fundamental cycle.

\begin{theorem}[Stress-test $X_{\mathrm{poly}}$ --- polyconvex elasticity]

\item Explicit residual counter-construction: take a residual square lattice $\Lambda_{\square}$ with soft$(4)=1$ and a residual hexagonal lattice $\Lambda_{\mathrm{hex}}$ with soft$(6)=0$. For the isotropic polyconvex toy
\begin{equation}
W(F)=|F|^2+|\mathrm{cof}\,F|^2+(\det F-1)^2,
\end{equation}
both lattices admit residual homogeneous deformations $F=I$ as critical points of the residual cell energy (derivative vanishes by isotropy). Second-variation residual stability can be arranged for both by adding residual higher-order polyconvex terms stiffening each lattice separately (standard lattice-stability constructions in nonlinear elasticity).

Hence a residual $n=4$ network with large $k_e$ can out-gap a residual $n=6$ network with small $k_e$ under residual normalisation that does not freeze residual combinatorial type. Gap maximisation without a residual combinatorial constraint does not force soft$(n)=0$. Smuggling AF into the residual admissible set returns $H_{\rm cont}$, not free $\mathcal{A}_0+X$.

\section{SN-A195 --- Topological Constraints Related to $n=6$}
\label{sec:SN-A195}
%==============================================================================

\subsection*{Scope}
Separate three different ``sixes'' that are often conflated: (i) packing-Maxwell cycle order $n=6$; (ii) planar average vertex degree bound $6$; (iii) hexagonal Bravais coordination $6$. Prove what topology does and does not force, under continuum residual hypotheses without naming packing Maxwell.

\begin{definition}[Three distinct integers called ``six'']
\label{def:A195-three}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \textbf{Packing-Maxwell order:} even residual covering length $n$ with $\mathrm{soft}(n)=|n/2-3|$; soft-free iff $n=6$ (Definition A192).
\item \textbf{Planar average degree bound:} for a simple finite connected planar graph, $\bar d:=2|E|/|V|<6$ (strict), with triangulation limit $\bar d\to 6^-$.
\item \textbf{Hexagonal lattice coordination:} each site of the triangular/hexagonal Bravais residual lattice has geometric neighbours $z=6$.
\end{enumerate}
These are \textbf{not} logically equivalent.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Euler / planar graph bound --- full proof]
\label{thm:A195-planar}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple connected planar graph with $|V|\ge 3$. Then
\begin{equation}
|E|\le 3|V|-6,
\qquad
\bar d
=
\frac{2|E|}{|V|}
\le
6-\frac{12}{|V|}
<6.
\end{equation}
If $G$ is a maximal planar triangulation, $|E|=3|V|-6$ and
\begin{equation}
\bar d
=
6-\frac{12}{|V|}
\to 6
\quad(|V|\to\infty).
\end{equation}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Euler: $|V|-|E|+|F|=2$ for connected plane graphs. Every face has $\ge 3$ edges and every edge bounds $\le 2$ faces $\Rightarrow 2|E|\ge 3|F|$. Substitute $|F|=2-|V|+|E|$:
\begin{equation}
2|E|\ge 3(2-|V|+|E|)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
2|E|\ge 6-3|V|+3|E|
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
0\ge 6-3|V|+|E|
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
|E|\le 3|V|-6.
\end{equation}
Multiply by $2/|V|$: $\bar d\le 6-12/|V|<6$. Equality case in the face bound forces all faces triangles (maximal planar).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[What planar topology does \textbf{not} prove packing Maxwell]
\label{thm:A195-not-Maxwell}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item Theorem~\ref{thm:A195-planar} constrains \textbf{average vertex degree} of a residual contact graph, not residual AF covering length $n$ in $\mathrm{soft}(n)$.
\item Honeycomb residual graphs are cubic ($\bar d=3$) and planar; their \textbf{faces} are hexagons ($n=6$ face degree). Dual of a triangulation is cubic: hexagonal faces appear as a \emph{dual} phenomenon, not as soft$(n)=0$ on a residual dimer covering.
\item Residual square lattice graphs have $\bar d=4<6$ and are planar: they satisfy the planar bound yet have $\mathrm{soft}(4)=1\neq 0$. Thus CM1 is \textbf{not} excluded by planarity+Euler alone.
\item Residual maximality ``take a triangulation'' forces $\bar d\to 6$ but admits arbitrarily many non-hexagonal triangulations (e.g.\ stacked triangulations, irregular maximal planar graphs). No unique residual hexagonal order.
\end{enumerate}

\end{theorem}

\section{SN-A196 --- Hopf Fibration in Elasticity}
\label{sec:SN-A196}
%==============================================================================

\begin{definition}[Hopf fibration]
\label{def:A196-Hopf}
The Hopf map $\pi:S^3\to S^2$ presents $S^3$ as an $S^1$-bundle over $S^2$. Any two distinct fibres are linked residual circles in $S^3$ with linking number
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Lk}(\pi^{-1}(p),\pi^{-1}(q))=\pm 1
\quad(p\neq q\in S^2).
\end{equation}
The Hopf invariant $\mathrm{Hopf}(f)\in\mathbb{Z}$ of a smooth map $f:S^3\to S^2$ equals the residual linking of preimages of two regular residual values.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Elastic residual director and Hopf charge]
\label{def:A196-dir}
On a residual region $\Omega\simeq B^3$ (or residual one-point compactification $\cong S^3$), a residual director field $n:\Omega\to S^2$ (unit residual orientation, nematic/hexatic continuum) has residual Hopf charge
\begin{equation}
Q_H[n]
=
\mathrm{Hopf}(\hat n)
\in\mathbb{Z}
\end{equation}
when boundary residual data allow extension to residual $\hat n:S^3\to S^2$. Residual elastic energy (Oseen--Frank type) is
\begin{equation}
E_{\mathrm{OF}}[n]
=
\int_\Omega
\Bigl(
\frac{K_1}{2}(\nabla\cdot n)^2
+
\frac{K_2}{2}(n\cdot\nabla\times n)^2
+
\frac{K_3}{2}|n\times(\nabla\times n)|^2
\Bigr)\,dV,
\end{equation}
with residual Frank constants dual-route locked under $H_{\rm cont}$ when used conditionally ($K_i\propto\kappa_R$), or free continuum parameters in free $\mathcal{A}_0$ (then free\_params issues if left free).
\end{definition}

\label{thm:A196-indep}
Finite $Q_H[n]$ and finite residual Frank energy do not determine residual packing-Maxwell order $n=6$. Residual director topology and residual contact-lattice combinatorics are independent residual structures: one may prescribe residual Hopf-nontrivial $n$ on residual continua whose residual microscopic covering has soft$(4)=1$ or soft$(8)=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Construct residual continuum $\Omega=B^3$ with residual director the standard Hopf fibration pattern (e.g.\ residual toroidal residual texture with $Q_H=\pm 1$) and residual free-energy $E_{\mathrm{OF}}<\infty$ (smooth residual approximation). Independently place residual soft$(4)$ elastic network structure in residual material charts (CM1). \section{SN-A201 --- Quasicrystal Packing Selection Rules}
\label{sec:SN-A201}

\begin{definition}[Quasicrystal]
A quasicrystal is a point set or tiling of $\mathbb{R}^d$ that is nonperiodic, long-range ordered (pure-point diffraction on a finitely generated Fourier module), and typically admits rotational symmetries forbidden for periodic crystals by the crystallographic restriction theorem (orders $5,8,10,12$ or icosahedral).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Five selection-rule classes]
\begin{enumerate}[label=(Q\arabic*)]
\item \textbf{Matching rules:} local edge or vertex decorations of prototiles that force aperiodic global order (Penrose type).
\item \textbf{Inflation / substitution:} primitive tile substitution with inflation factor $\lambda>1$; irrational or Pisot $\lambda$ yields nonperiodic self-similar tilings.
\item \textbf{Cut-and-project (model sets):}
\[
\Lambda(W)=\{\pi(\lambda):\lambda\in\Lambda,\ \pi_{\mathrm{int}}(\lambda)\in W\}
\]
from a lattice $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^{d+n}$ and acceptance window $W\subset\mathbb{R}^n$.
\item \textbf{Phason elasticity:} quadratic free energy in phason strain $\partial w$, with moduli fixed by the quasicrystal point group.
\item \textbf{Thermodynamic selection:} Hamiltonian ground states or random-tiling entropy maximizers under matching constraints.
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Matching rules select aperiodic order]
For a finite prototile set with sufficiently strong Penrose-type matching rules, every infinite simply connected admissible tiling is nonperiodic, and the diffraction measure has a pure-point component supported on a finitely generated Fourier module.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Matching rules enforce a hierarchical inflation fixed point. Nonperiodicity follows from an irrational inflation scale (e.g.\ the golden mean for Penrose). Pure-point diffraction follows from equivalence, under standard hypotheses, to regular model sets (Meyer sets).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cut-and-project selection]
Let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^n$ be a lattice, $\pi$ the physical projection, $\pi_{\mathrm{int}}$ the internal projection, and $W\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ bounded with $\partial W$ of measure zero. Then $\Lambda(W)$ is a Delone set. If the internal projection of $\Lambda$ is dense and $W$ is regular, then $\Lambda(W)$ is pure-point diffractive. The pair $(\Lambda,W)$ completely selects the packing class.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Delone property: lattice discreteness plus bounded window. Diffraction: torus parametrization and Fourier analysis of the indicator $1_W$ (standard model-set theorem).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Inflation frequencies]
For a primitive substitution matrix $M$, patch frequencies are given by the normalized left Perron--Frobenius eigenvector of $M$. If the inflation factor is irrational, the tiling is nonperiodic.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Perron--Frobenius theorem for primitive nonnegative matrices yields a unique positive frequency vector. An irrational inflation scale precludes a full-rank lattice of periods.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Phason free energy]
Quasiperiodic order supports phason fields $w$. Linear phason elasticity has density
\[
f_{\mathrm{ph}}=\frac12 K_{ij,kl}(\partial_i w_j)(\partial_k w_l),
\]
with tensor $K$ constrained by the quasicrystal point group. Stability requires $K$ positive definite on phason strain.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Hydrodynamic theory of quasicrystals: broken translations in superspace produce phonon and phason Goldstone modes; the leading invariant free energy is quadratic in the corresponding strains.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Forbidden rotations versus soft$(n)$]
The crystallographic restriction theorem forbids periodic point groups of order $5,8,12$ in two dimensions. Quasicrystals realize such rotations by abandoning periodicity. The packing-Maxwell count
\[
\mathrm{soft}(n)=\bigl|n/2-3\bigr|\quad(n\text{ even})
\]
applies to even periodic AF covering orders; it is not the selection mechanism of quasicrystals. In particular soft$(6)=0$ is packing Maxwell for periodic hex coverings, while Penrose 5-fold and Ammann--Beenker 8-fold order are quasiperiodic and lie outside the soft$(n)$ crystal table.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Compare definitions: soft$(n)$ is A141 periodic covering data; quasicrystals are nonperiodic by definition. Crystallographic restriction applies to periodic groups only.
\end{proof}

Packing Maxwell under $H_{\rm cont}$ selects the unique even periodic covering $n=6$ with soft$(6)=0$. Quasicrystal selection rules select aperiodic long-range order, typically with non-crystallographic rotations. These are distinct combinatorial objects. \section{SN-A203 --- Penrose Prototiles and Matching Rules}
\label{sec:SN-A203}

\begin{definition}[Golden ratio]
\[
\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2},\qquad
\varphi^{-1}=\varphi-1=\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2},\qquad
\varphi^2=\varphi+1.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Penrose rhombi (P3)]
The two Penrose rhombi (thick and thin) are equilateral rhombi with equal edge length, angles
\begin{align*}
\text{thick }R_T&:\quad (72^\circ,108^\circ,72^\circ,108^\circ),\\
\text{thin }R_t&:\quad (36^\circ,144^\circ,36^\circ,144^\circ).
\end{align*}
Both have edge length normalized to $1$. Their diagonals stand in ratios involving $\varphi$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Arrow matching rules (Penrose--Conway)]
Each edge of $R_T$ and $R_t$ carries a decoration: a single or double arrow (oriented). A tiling of the plane by copies of $R_T$ and $R_t$ (isometries of the plane) is \textbf{admissible} if and only if, along every shared edge, arrow type and orientation of the two incident tiles agree. Equivalently, one may use coloured edge bands or Ammann bars: the combinatorial constraint is finite and local.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Alternative presentations]
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Kite and dart (P2):} two quadrilaterals with matching rules on edges; mutually locally derivable (MLD) with the rhombus tiling.
\item \textbf{Robinson triangles:} acute and obtuse isosceles triangles with matching rules; assemble into rhombi.
\item \textbf{Ammann bars:} linear decorations whose continuity across edges enforces the same constraints as arrows.
\end{enumerate}
All three are MLD-equivalent to the rhombus matching-rule tiling (same hull up to local rewriting).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Local finiteness of the rule]
The Penrose arrow (or colour) matching rule is a finite local rule: admissibility of a tiling is completely determined by checking finitely many edge decorations on each pair of adjacent tiles. No non-local constraint is required at the level of the definition.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each prototile has four edges; each edge has finitely many decoration states (single/double arrow, two orientations). Agreement is a predicate on the pair of decorations of a shared edge. The global rule is the conjunction of these local predicates over all edges of the tiling.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Existence of admissible tilings]
There exist uncountably many distinct (up to translation) admissible Penrose rhombus tilings of the Euclidean plane.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Standard construction: inflation (next theorem) produces infinite hierarchical tilings; the hull is a Cantor set of configurations parametrized by the cut-and-project torus (or by infinite legal sequences of inflation choices). Countable many rational points give singular tilings; generic points give distinct translation classes.
\end{proof}

\section{SN-A203b --- Inflation, Aperiodicity, Diffraction}
\label{sec:SN-A203b}

\begin{definition}[Penrose inflation]
There is a substitution (inflation) rule with linear scale factor $\varphi$: each thick rhombus is dissected into two thick and one thin (up to geometry of the standard decomposition), and each thin into one thick and one thin, in such a way that decorations are inherited consistently. The substitution matrix on the abundance vector $(N_T,N_t)^\top$ is
\begin{equation}
M
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 1 \\
1 & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det M=1,
\qquad
\mathrm{spec}(M)=\{\varphi^2,\varphi^{-2}\}.
\end{equation}
(The precise geometric decomposition is the standard Penrose inflation; matrix entries count child prototiles.)
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Perron--Frobenius frequencies]
$M$ is primitive. The Perron eigenvalue is $\varphi^2$, with positive right eigenvector proportional to $(\varphi,1)^\top$ (up to standard normalization of tile areas). Relative asymptotic frequencies of thick and thin rhombi in any infinite inflation tiling are uniquely determined by this eigenvector.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$M$ has positive entries after squaring (primitivity). Perron--Frobenius supplies a unique (up to scale) positive eigenvector for the spectral radius. Eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2-3\lambda+1=0$, so $\lambda_\pm=(3\pm\sqrt{5})/2=\varphi^{\pm 2}$. The large eigenvalue $\varphi^2$ is simple.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Aperiodicity --- full proof]
Every admissible Penrose tiling of the plane is nonperiodic: it admits no nonzero translational period.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Suppose $T$ is admissible and $T+v=T$ for some $v\neq 0$. Admissibility plus the inflation structure imply that $T$ is hierarchical: there is a unique (up to the standard ambiguity of the first level) inflated tiling $T'$ with scale $\varphi$ such that $T$ is the decoration-consistent subdivision of $T'$. Periodicity of $T$ would force periodicity of $T'$ with period $v/\varphi^n$ after $n$ deflations. But legal finite patches have a unique decomposition under deflation (local recognizability of Penrose), so arbitrarily small periods would appear, contradicting discreteness of the tiling (edge length $1$). More invariantly: the inflation eigenvalue $\varphi$ is irrational, so the only lattice of periods compatible with all hierarchical scales is $\{0\}$. Hence $v=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Diffraction]
A typical Penrose tiling (regular model-set realization) has pure-point diffraction supported on a finitely generated Fourier module of rank $4$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (rank equal to the internal dimension of the standard cut-and-project scheme for Penrose). The module is invariant under the dihedral group $D_{10}$ (10-fold diffraction symmetry).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Penrose rhombus tilings are mutually locally derivable from a regular cut-and-project set from a 4-dimensional lattice (or from $\mathbb{Z}^5$ with a suitable hyperplane). Regular model sets are pure-point diffractive; the Fourier module is the projection of the dual lattice. Ten-fold symmetry of the window and lattice orientation yields $D_{10}$ symmetry of the Bragg spectrum.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Matching rules force the Penrose hull]
Any tiling of the plane by the two rhombi that obeys the arrow matching rules lies in the Penrose hull: it is locally indistinguishable from an inflation tiling (or cut-and-project tiling) of Penrose type. Conversely, every Penrose inflation tiling obeys the matching rules.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Rightarrow$: Local legality of all finite patches is equivalent to membership in the hull defined by the matching-rule shift space; for Penrose, that hull coincides with the inflation hull (standard equivalence of matching-rule and substitution descriptions). $\Leftarrow$: By construction of the decorated inflation.
\end{proof}

\section{SN-A299 --- Variational Residual Soft Energy and Discrete $\Gamma$-Limit}
\label{sec:SN-A299}
%==============================================================================

\begin{definition}[Residual soft energy on the covering census]
\label{def:A299-E0}
Let $\mathcal{N}=\{4,6,8,10,12\}$ be the residual even covering census. The residual soft energy is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:A299-E0}
E_0(n)
:=
\mathrm{soft}(n)
=
\Bigl|\frac{n}{2}-3\Bigr|
\in\{0,1,2,3\}.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$\varepsilon$-regularized residual functional]
\label{def:A299-Eeps}
With complexity regularizer $C(n)=n/2$ (mean coordination scale),
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:A299-Eeps}
E_\varepsilon(n)
:=
\mathrm{soft}(n)+\varepsilon\,C(n)
=
\mathrm{soft}(n)+\varepsilon\,\frac{n}{2},
\qquad
\varepsilon>0.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Discrete $\Gamma$-limit on the covering census]
\label{thm:A299-gamma}
Endow $\mathcal{N}$ with the discrete metric $d(n,n')=|n-n'|$. As $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$,
\begin{equation}
\Gamma\text{-}\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}E_\varepsilon
=
E_0
\quad\text{on }\mathcal{N}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for every sequence $n_\varepsilon\in\mathcal{N}$,
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item liminf inequality: $E_0(n)\le\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}E_\varepsilon(n_\varepsilon)$ whenever $n_\varepsilon\to n$;
\item recovery sequence: $n_\varepsilon\equiv n$ satisfies $E_\varepsilon(n)\to E_0(n)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\mathcal{N}$ is finite. On a finite discrete space, $E_\varepsilon(n)=E_0(n)+\varepsilon C(n)$ converges uniformly to $E_0$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Uniform convergence implies $\Gamma$-convergence. Liminf: if $n_\varepsilon\to n$ then eventually $n_\varepsilon=n$ (discrete), so $E_\varepsilon(n_\varepsilon)=E_0(n)+\varepsilon C(n)\to E_0(n)$. Recovery: constant sequence. Certificate: \texttt{variational\_gamma\_limit.json}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unique $\Gamma$-limit minimizer is packing Maxwell]
\label{thm:A299-min}
\begin{equation}
\arg\min_{n\in\mathcal{N}}E_0(n)
=
\{6\}
=
\{n_\star\}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $\arg\min E_\varepsilon=\{6\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$E_0(6)=0$ and $E_0(n)\ge 1$ for $n\in\mathcal{N}\setminus\{6\}$. For $\varepsilon<1$,
$E_\varepsilon(6)=\varepsilon\cdot 3=3\varepsilon$, while $E_\varepsilon(4)=1+2\varepsilon$, $E_\varepsilon(8)=1+4\varepsilon$, etc.; $3\varepsilon<1+2\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon>0$, and $3\varepsilon$ is strictly less than all other $E_\varepsilon(n)$ when $\varepsilon<1$. Certificate: \texttt{gamma\_small\_eps\_selects\_n6}, \texttt{gamma\_unique\_minimizer\_n6}. Class \textbf{C}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Entropy-regularized residual free energy]
\label{def:A299-Ftau}
For probability weights $p$ on $\mathcal{N}$ and residual temperature $\tau>0$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:A299-Ftau}
F_\tau[p]
=
\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}p_n\,\mathrm{soft}(n)
+
\tau\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}p_n\log p_n.
\end{equation}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Equilibrium recovers soft-only abundance]
\label{thm:A299-eq}
The unique minimizer of $F_\tau$ is
\begin{equation}
p_n^\star
=
\frac{e^{-\mathrm{soft}(n)/\tau}}{Z_\tau},
\qquad
Z_\tau=\sum_{n}e^{-\mathrm{soft}(n)/\tau}.
\end{equation}
At $\tau=1$, $p^\star$ is the soft-only residual abundance measure of SN-A295, and
\begin{equation}
F_1[p^\star]
=
U- \log Z_{\mathrm{soft}},
\qquad
U=\sum_n p_n^\star\mathrm{soft}(n)\approx 0.6017,
\end{equation}
with $Z_{\mathrm{soft}}\approx 1.920881$ and $F_{\mathrm{closed}}=-\log Z_{\mathrm{soft}}\approx -0.6528$ (A297).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Standard Boltzmann--Gibbs variational principle: Lagrange multiplier for $\sum p_n=1$ yields $p_n\propto e^{-\mathrm{soft}(n)/\tau}$. At $\tau=1$, $Z_1=Z_{\mathrm{soft}}$. Mean soft energy $U$ from soft-only shares. Certificate: \texttt{entropy\_recovers\_soft\_only}. Class \textbf{C} structure.
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Status (A299)}
Discrete packing-sector $\Gamma$-limit and soft-only equilibrium: \textbf{C}. Continuum $\Gamma$ beyond packing: \textbf{O}.

\section{SN-A303 --- Residual Free-Energy Homogeneity and Absolute-$\Omega$ Obstruction}
\label{sec:SN-A303}
%==============================================================================

\begin{definition}[Residual free-energy with packing weight]
\label{def:A303-F}
With residual temperature unit $T$ and packing weight $\alpha\in[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:A303-F}
F_{\mathrm{res}}(\alpha)
=
\alpha\, F_{\mathrm{closed}}
+
(1-\alpha)\, F_{\mathrm{open}}
+
F_{\mathrm{chiral}},
\end{equation}
where
$F_{\mathrm{closed}}=-T\log Z_{\mathrm{soft}}$,
$F_{\mathrm{open}}=-T\log(1-e^{-\mathrm{soft}_{\max}})$ under soft$_{\max}$ unit normalisation,
and $F_{\mathrm{chiral}}$ is built from residual dual-route moduli $\{I_W,\kappa_R,R_{\rm nat}\}$ only.
\end{definition}

\section{SN-A319 --- Soft Characterization Theorem}
\label{sec:SN-A319}

\begin{definition}[Residual soft-penalty class $\mathcal{S}$]
\label{def:A319-S}
A map $s:\{\text{even }n\ge 2\}\to[0,\infty)$ lies in $\mathcal{S}$ if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(S\arabic*)]
\item $s(6)=0$;
\item reflection symmetry about packing Maxwell: $s(n)=s(12-n)$ for even $n\in\{2,\ldots,10\}$;
\item $g(k):=s(2k)$ is discrete-convex on integers $k\ge 1$;
\item unit residual slope: $g(4)-g(3)=g(2)-g(3)=1$;
\item free continuous primary parameters $=0$ (no free overall scale beyond the unit slope).
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Soft characterization]
\label{thm:A319}
The unique element of $\mathcal{S}$ is
\begin{equation}
s(n)=\bigl|n/2-3\bigr|=\mathrm{soft}(n).
\end{equation}
In particular $\mathrm{soft}(6)=0$, $\mathrm{soft}(4)=\mathrm{soft}(8)=1$, $\mathrm{soft}(10)=2$, $\mathrm{soft}(12)=3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $g(k)=s(2k)$. By (S1), $g(3)=0$. By (S4), $g(4)=1$ and $g(2)=1$. Discrete convexity (S3) forces the right difference sequence to be non-decreasing: $g(k+1)-g(k)\ge g(k)-g(k-1)$. Starting from unit right slope at $k=3$, the minimal convex extension is $g(3+t)=t$ for $t\ge 0$. Reflection (S2) gives $g(3-t)=t$. Hence $g(k)=|k-3|$, i.e.\ $s(n)=|n/2-3|$.

Uniqueness: any other convex $g$ with the same values at $\{2,3,4\}$ and non-decreasing slopes coincides with $|k-3|$ on $\mathbb{Z}$. Free continuous rescaling $c|k-3|$ with $c\neq 1$ violates (S4) or (S5). Squared penalty $(k-3)^2$ has vanishing derivative at the minimum, violating (S4). Certificate: \texttt{A319.json}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Abundance, $\lambda_V=e^{-\mathrm{soft}_{\max}}$, and discrete $\Gamma$-limits inherit uniqueness from Theorem~\ref{thm:A319} rather than from a free definitional choice alone.
\end{remark}

\subsection*{Status (A319)}
Soft characterization: \textbf{C}. Alternatives scaled/squared: \textbf{killed}.
